title: Tewarie: Economy still treading water, with no  clear path to recovery
summary: Pro Vice Chancellor for Planning and Development at The University of the West Indies Dr Bhoe Tewarie has described the country’s economic position as one in which the Government was struggling to stay afloat while attempting to move against difficult economic currents.
author: Verdel Bishop
content:
Dr Bhoe Tewarie
Pro Vice Chancellor for Planning and Development at The University of the West Indies Dr Bhoe Tewarie has described the country’s economic position as one in which the Government was struggling to stay afloat while attempting to move against difficult economic currents.
Speaking at a virtual discussion hosted by The University of the West Indies’ Trade and Development Economic Unit (TEDU) on Friday night, the former government minister said the country’s economic challenges would not disappear even if natural gas production increased through upcoming projects. He said: “This is a budget which says to the country that we are going to find a way to float, and right now we just have to tread water and float. We can’t do much more than that. We know that we will need a lifeboat, and we know that we need time because it is not on our side, but little by little we will get there.”
Tewarie said the Government had inherited a difficult economic situation and had taken steps to stabilise the economy, including measures to improve tax collection, strengthen Customs enforcement and broaden financial inclusion.
However, he said those measures had not yet translated into recovery or a clear growth path.
“The Government inherited an awful situation. I don’t think that can be argued against. They have met the challenge and stabilised the economy, but there is no recovery and there is no clear growth path,” he said.
Tewarie also warned that approximately $70 billion in existing public debt would fall due within the next five years, creating a significant refinancing challenge.
He cautioned that efforts to increase foreign exchange earnings through exports and import substitution would not necessarily increase the country’s overall supply of foreign exchange.
“It is the same pool of forex that you are dealing with; you are not increasing it. It is only a redirection of what is in the pool,” he said.
Tewarie said diversification, investment and exports remained major challenges, with limited growth in exports and insufficient investment in new areas of economic activity.
He also raised concern about the country’s political climate, warning that confrontational rhetoric was adding to the pressures facing citizens.
“The economic climate is extremely challenging. The financial system situation, in my view, is equivalent to one of entrapment. And the political climate, in my view, is much too adversarial. It is much too confrontational,” he said.
Tewarie warned that racial tensions were also surfacing.
“I think some of the political rhetoric is stoking racial polarisation and creating the conditions for instability in Trinidad and Tobago,” he said.
He urged both the Government and Opposition to be more measured in their public statements.
“I would advise that both the Government and the Opposition be much more judicious in the way they manage the tone of the politics and the language of engagement as we navigate this very, very difficult period in Trinidad and Tobago’s economic and political history,” he said.
‘Hung out to dry’
Also speaking at the virtual event, businessman Vivek Charran said small and medium-sized enterprises had felt the effects of the economic downturn over the past decade and needed greater support to become part of the country’s diversification drive.
“As someone who’s been representing SMEs and as an owner of a family business as well, we acutely felt the downturn, the contraction of the economy over those last, let’s say, ten years. We felt that we weren’t being listened to. We felt that we were being hung out to dry, that we were being abandoned in a sense, and we were being marginalised and blamed for things that really weren’t within our responsibility,” he said.
Charran said the budget did not contain direct delivery for SMEs, but argued that small businesses had an important role to play in building the non-energy sector.
“More than ever, what the opportunity presents itself in the economy for is taking the risk to diversify as a way to survive, augment your current income flow and prepare for the future,” he said.
He identified access to financing as one of the biggest barriers facing small businesses seeking to enter manufacturing.
“One of the first barriers is actually getting finance from the commercial banks,” Charran said, explaining that many SMEs were already carrying debt, facing lower sales and struggling with cash flow.
He said banks often required collateral valued at one and a half to two times the amount being invested, making it difficult for smaller businesses to obtain financing for expansion.
Charran also called for greater investment in agriculture and food production, arguing that reducing imports was just as important as earning foreign exchange.
“We often talk about what can we do as an economy to earn more forex. But equally important is what do we need to do as an economy to save forex?” he said.
He pointed to the country’s dairy import bill, estimated at between $300 million and $350 million annually, and said local producers had opportunities to supply more of the domestic market.
“If we can attract investment into dairy and then start to produce our own milk, increase our milk production, that is an opportunity,” he said.
Charran said SMEs could also explore egg production, broiler farming, leafy greens and hydroponics to meet local demand and reduce dependence on imported food.
He further noted that businesses could not simply wait for Government intervention while the economy was being rebuilt.
“Asking the Government alone what they could do or what they’re doing with the economy is not enough. We need to ask ourselves what are we prepared to do to ensure our survival and to initiate some growth for ourselves,” he said.

title: Nagar opens amid controversy as Mangaroo preaches unity
summary: National Council of Indian Culture (NCIC) president Surujdeo Mangaroo emphasised unity, appreciation and preservation of culture as he opened the annual nine-night Divali Nagar in Chaguanas on Friday.
author: Susan Mohammed
content:
Opening-night token: NCIC president Surujdeo Mangaroo, left, presents Speaker of the National Assembly of Guyana Manzoor Nadir with a plaque at the opening night of Divali Nagar, on Friday in Chaguanas. See Page 9.
—Photos: ISHMAEL SALANDY
National Council of Indian Culture (NCIC) president Surujdeo Mangaroo emphasised unity, appreciation and preservation of culture as he opened the annual nine-night Divali Nagar in Chaguanas on Friday.
In his opening address, Mangaroo did not directly address board resignations, sponsorships, or the Prime Minister’s criticism of the NCIC. Instead he emphasised cooperation and voluntary service that are required to stage the annual cultural celebration.
“Divali Nagar does not happen by chance. It happens because people give their time, their energy and their hearts to something bigger than themselves and I would like to publicly thank my elected board of directors for their support and loyalty,” he said.
“To our merchants and exhibitors, thank you for bringing your products, your creativity and your enterprise. To our artistes, musicians, dancers and performers, thank you for keeping our traditions alive through your talent. And to our hundreds of volunteers, the many people who work quietly, often behind the scenes and without recognition, I offer a special word of gratitude.”
The NCIC president also acknowledged corporate sponsors, partners and supporters whose contributions, he said, helped make the “national undertaking” possible.
The annual event opened on Friday night against the backdrop of the departures of appointed board members Dr Shane Mohammed, Ferida Ramkissoon and Varsha Ramharrack.
‘Discerning Truth
in an Age of AI’
In his address on opening night of Divali Nagar 2026, the NCIC president focused on the Nagar’s theme, “Viveka: Discerning Truth in an Age of AI”, urging citizens to exercise judgment in distinguishing truth from falsehood and right from wrong.
He described Viveka, a concept in Hindu philosophy, as more than the ability to acquire knowledge.
“It is not simply the ability to know more. It is the wisdom to know what matters,” he said.
The NCIC president said advances in artificial intelligence had transformed research, communication and business, but the ability of machines to generate information did not remove the need for human scrutiny.
“Because information is available, does that mean it is true? And because technology makes something possible, does that necessarily make it right?” he asked.
He said such questions required human judgment, warning that technological progress should be accompanied by moral responsibility.
“Our theme is not an argument against artificial intelligence,” Mangaroo said, noting its potential to assist children, doctors, farmers and businesses. “The issue is whether we can embrace it without surrendering our judgment, our values and our humanity.”
He urged parents and educators to teach children to question and verify information, respect others and understand the consequences of their actions.
A computer could assist with an assignment, said Mangaroo, but could not replace a child’s intellectual development. Similarly, technology could generate words of sympathy without replacing the human act of supporting someone in distress.
“We can have the brightest screens and still make the darkest decisions,” he said. “Let us welcome innovation, but never abandon discernment. Let us give our children the tools of the future while grounding them in the values that make any future worth living.
“As Trinidad and Tobago embraces the opportunities of a rapidly changing world, let us ensure that our technological progress is accompanied by moral progress. That is one of the reasons Divali Nagar matters,” he said.
Appreciating
Indian culture
Turning to the significance of the festival, Mangaroo said Divali Nagar offered more than shopping, food and entertainment. It provided a meeting place for generations and an opportunity for the wider population to appreciate Indian culture’s contribution to Trinidad and Tobago.
He said its success depended on cooperation among volunteers, merchants, artistes, sponsors, institutions and the public.
“To everyone who has helped bring this year’s Nagar to life, thank you. You are not simply organising an event. You are helping to preserve a living inheritance and pass it on to another generation,” he said.
“May you enjoy the festivities, celebrate our culture, support our exhibitors and performers, and leave with a deeper appreciation of the wisdom our heritage offers the modern world.”

title: I’LL KEEP FIGHTING FOR YOU
summary: Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has vowed to continue fighting for the people of Trinidad and Tobago, declaring that her Government has a duty to confront crime, corruption and neglect while ensuring that no community is left behind.
author: Anna Ramdass
content:
Divali puja: Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar, centre, takes part in a Divali puja led by a pundit at her Siparia constituency office yesterday.
—Photo courtesy the Prime Minister’s Facebook page
Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has vowed to continue fighting for the people of Trinidad and Tobago, declaring that her Government has a duty to confront crime, corruption and neglect while ensuring that no community is left behind.
Speaking at the 29th annual Divali celebrations at her Siparia constituency office last night, Persad-Bissessar pledged to deliver safer communities, reliable public services and greater opportunities for families.
“No community should have to plead to be seen by its own Government,” she said.
“Reliable water, accessible healthcare, properly maintained roads, education, and opportunities to earn are the foundations upon which families build secure lives.”
She said the recent national budget and the work of Government ministries must deliver tangible improvements, particularly in communities that have waited longest.
“We accept the responsibility to pursue it with urgency, because delay is felt in someone’s home, livelihood or hopes for a child,” she said.
Warning that crime could destroy livelihoods, shatter families and rob neighbourhoods of peace, Persad-Bissessar declared: “Our action against crime, corruption and neglect must defend the dignity and security of those we serve.”
Persad-Bissessar noted that earlier in the day the pundit asked her what does the flame represent and she responded it was the heart.
She said he said it was, in fact, the tongue which must be used to speak out for righteousness.
Persad-Bissessar vowed never to stop speaking and fighting for people.
“For my Government, Divali’s promise must be expressed in ­safer communities, effective services, and opportunities that families can see and grasp,” she said.
The celebration was attended by several diplomats, including Venezuelan Ambassador Álvaro Enrique Sánchez Cordero. who heads the diplomatic corps, Oilfields Workers’ Trade Union (OWTU) president Ancel Roget, and most members of the Cabinet.
Outstanding citizens recognised
The Prime Minister used the occasion to recognise outstanding citizens whose contributions have strengthened their communities.
Cricketer Amrita Ramtahal and football contributor Darrel Garcia were honoured for inspiring young people through dedication and ­discipline.
Carmina Hosein was recognised for decades of sewing, craftsmanship, teaching and voluntary service; while Vijai Bridglal was honoured for his contributions to public service, transportation and community involvement.
Denesh Tarsoo received recognition for his work in agriculture.
Outstanding students Aurea Mahabir, Devina Dodal, Kadir Chung and Kavir Newton were also celebrated for their academic achievements.
“Your achievements show what communities can accomplish when their people are encouraged,” Persad-Bissessar said, adding, “Government must help ensure that such opportunity reaches every single child.”
Childhood reflections
Reflecting on her own childhood, the Prime Minister recalled standing alongside her grandmother, affectionately known as Aagie, selling bodi and other vegetables at the Penal Market, directly opposite the venue.
“Amid that hustle and bustle, I could never have imagined that one day I would stand across this very road as Prime Minister, celebrating Divali with the children and grandchildren of the people who helped raise me,” she said.
Those farmers and vendors, she recalled, earned modest incomes but carried immense hopes for their children.
“I am one of the children who benefited from their sacrifice,” she said.
“I owe the people who raised me more than remembrance. I owe them service, and I owe their children the chance that their sacrifices gave me.”
She recalled how earlier generations pooled their limited resources to establish schools and places of worship, including humble schools described as “cow sheds”.
Persad-Bissessar, who ­attended the Mohess Road Hindu School, said Trinidad and Tobago’s strength lay in its diverse ancestral roots and shared national identity.
She thanked the Siparia Women’s Association, religious leaders, sponsors, donors, teachers, students and volunteers for sustaining the celebrations and community outreach programmes, including hamper distributions, toy drives, health clinics and legal clinics.
The Prime Minister also expressed appreciation to diplomats who travelled from Port of Spain to attend Divali celebrations in Couva and Siparia.
Persad-Bissessar also paid tribute to her husband, Dr Gregory Bissessar, whom she said was unable to attend because injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident during last year’s general election campaign continued to affect his mobility.
“His great spirit and immense brainpower remain strong. Through the demands and difficulties of public life, he remains my rock and a steady light,” she said.
She thanked him for his courage, patience and unwavering love, declaring that she could not have made her political journey without him.
Victories and defeats
Reflecting on her 31 years as Siparia MP, Persad-Bissessar thanked constituents for standing by her through political victories and defeats.
Recalling her return to the prime ministership last year after a decade in opposition, she said constituents had lifted their deyas to welcome their leader home.
“Tonight, I renew my pledge to you—you will have my service, my strength and my heart to the end of my days, I always say—half of me belongs to you; the other half, I give to you.”
She pledged to honour their trust through her decisions, her work and her continued service, ensuring that future generations would have opportunities greater than those available to their parents and grandparents.

title: Sinanan: No wrongdoing reports against former-PURE deputy
summary: Former works and transport minister Rohan Sinanan says no concerns about former Programme for Upgrading Roads Efficiency (PURE) Deputy Director Hayden Phillip were ever brought to his attention during his time in office.
content:
No concerns raised: Rohan Sinanan
Former works and transport minister Rohan Sinanan says no concerns about former Programme for Upgrading Roads Efficiency (PURE) Deputy Director Hayden Phillip were ever brought to his attention during his time in office.
Asked for comment on the dismissal of Phillip over allegations of “gross misconduct, malfeasance, misbehaviour in public office and breaches of contract” outlined in a termination letter from the Ministry of Works and Infrastructure to him dated September 25, 2026, Sinanan told the Sunday Express on Friday, with regard to his tenure, “I cannot recall any instance or reports of wrongdoing drawn to my attention on the part of Deputy Director of PURE Hayden Phillip.”
He added that Phillip had assumed the deputy director role only in recent years and, to his knowledge, was appointed following an interview process conducted by the Ministry of Works and Infrastructure’s Human Resources Department.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has disclosed that criminal charges are likely to be brought against individuals following an investigation into PURE, which is being shut down after more than two decades of operations.
She also revealed that a separate investigation is under way into the expenditure of more than $750 million on just three miles of the Churchill-Roosevelt Highway Extension project under the former People’s National Movement (PNM) administration.
Persad-Bissessar said officials at the Ministry of Works and Transport and the National Infrastructure Development Company Ltd (Nidco) would have to answer questions about the highway project.
The closure of PURE was disclosed during the recent Standing Finance Committee proceedings in Parliament.
The programme, which has been in operation for more than 20 years, was established to undertake road rehabilitation and upgrading works across Trinidad and Tobago.
However, Persad-Bissessar has questioned its effectiveness, pointing to the country’s continuing road infrastructure problems despite decades of expenditure.
The Prime Minister did not identify the individuals under investigation, the nature of any suspected offences, or when charges might be laid.
With respect to the Churchill-Roosevelt Highway extension, Persad-Bissessar indicated the investigation would require explanations from officials at both the ministry and Nidco, which has been involved in the execution of major State infrastructure projects.
—with reporting by Mark Bassant
What pure was
responsible for:
According to the ministry’s published description, its responsibilities included six main areas:
1. Road rehabilitation: Upgrading and repairing existing roads, including local roads and roads requiring major intervention.
2. Traffic management: Expanding existing infrastructure to improve road capacity, reduce congestion and improve road safety.
3. Alternative access routes: Constructing temporary or alternative routes around road construction sites to reduce disruption.
4. Slope stabilisation: Repairing failed slopes and landslips to maintain access between communities.
5. Bridge construction and rehabilitation: Planning, designing, constructing and repairing bridges.
6. Pedestrian overpasses: Constructing overpasses to improve pedestrian safety.

title: PURE deputy  director  fired
summary: Deputy Programme Director of the Programme for Upgrading Roads Efficiency (PURE) Hayden Phillip has been fired over allegations of “gross misconduct, acts of malfeasance, misbehaviour in public office and fundamental breaches of contract”.
author: Mark Bassant
content:
Dismissed: Hayden Phillip, deputy director of PURE, Ministry of Works and Infrastructure.
Deputy Programme Director of the Programme for Upgrading Roads Efficiency (PURE) Hayden Phillip has been fired over allegations of “gross misconduct, acts of malfeasance, misbehaviour in public office and fundamental breaches of contract”.
He has been ordered to surrender all ministry and PURE property and barred from accessing ministry offices, databases, financial systems and official communication channels.
Highway project in spotlight:
Work on the extension of lanes on the
Sir Solomon Hochoy Highway, Chaguanas.
PURE, a unit of the Ministry of Works and Infrastructure (MOWI), was established in 2002, initially as a short-to medium-term programme to address the country’s deteriorating roads. It subsequently evolved into a major road infrastructure and project management unit, undertaking road rehabilitation, highway improvements, bridge construction, landslip repairs and other infrastructure projects throughout Trinidad.
Phillip’s dismissal follows several audits and internal investigations by the MOWI, which found systemic governance failures, procurement weaknesses, poor project oversight and other issues involving multimillion-dollar State contracts.
The MOWI further alleged Phillip’s appointment as deputy programme director had taken place without a recruitment process and had been influenced by a close relative at the ministry.
The ministry also stated that the findings had been referred to the Attorney General for advice and possible further action.
Via a detailed, 12-page termination letter signed by permanent secretary Ian Ramdahin on September 25, 2026, the ministry informed Phillip that his employment was being terminated with immediate effect. The decision followed a December 2025 enquiry which uncovered concerns that prompted further investigations by the ministry’s Internal Audit Department and the Central Audit Division of the Ministry of Finance, the letter stated.
Just before noon last Tuesday, the Sunday Express contacted Phillip by telephone for comment on the September 25 termination letter and the allegations outlined in it.
Phillip immediately responded: “I have no comment whatsoever.”
Pressed further to address the allegations in the letter, he repeated: “I have no comment whatsoever, and you know why. I have no comment whatsoever.”
Personal benefits?
One of the most serious allegations in the termination letter centred on claims of conflicts of interest and personal benefits allegedly received by Phillip from contractors awarded government contracts.
The MOWI also alleged Phillip maintained undisclosed corporate ties while serving as deputy director of PURE. Among the companies identified as being registered in Phillip’s name and those of two close relatives were Roads and Buildings Services Ltd, Lot #19 Villas Ltd and Omnia TT Ltd.
The letter described Lot #19 Villas Ltd as “A condominium located in the Villas at Millennium Lakes Limited, with an approximate value of $3.1 million”. It further alleged that the property had been transferred to Phillip by the directors of a contracting company.
The letter went on to remind Phillip that “the acceptance of any gift of significant monetary value in exchange for contract awards is an Internal Control risk that affects the MOWI inclusive of the PURE Unit”.
The contractor in question was awarded multimillion-dollar contracts under PURE.
Regarding Roads and Buildings Services Ltd, the ministry alleged “contractors have been provided business, material and labour in exchange for contract awards with the MOWI”.
The ministry also alleged that Phillip, who served as second-in-command of the road rehabilitation agency, had failed to implement adequate internal controls, establish standard operating procedures, maintain proper project governance systems, oversee procurement safeguards, manage contractual disputes and ensure appropriate reporting to the ministry’s accounting officers.
The ministry’s findings further stated that PURE operated with insufficient oversight despite managing hundreds of millions of dollars in public infrastructure projects.
According to the letter, PURE had no written standard operating procedures for project management, quality assurance, risk assessments, budget monitoring, contract administration, dispute resolution or project reporting.
The ministry said investigators found the PURE unit kept no written records and submitted no written reports to the MOWI, making oversight and audits difficult.
The letter further alleged PURE had failed to conduct financial risk assessments on major projects and lacked policies designed to prevent “financial impropriety, collusion, conflict of interest, fraud and/or unethical behaviour”.
According to the letter, investigators also identified what they described as a significant information gap between PURE and the ministry, potentially resulting in duplication of projects and the inefficient use of State funds.
Sir Solomon Hochoy Highway project
A substantial part of the MOWI investigation focused on the Sir Solomon Hochoy Highway project involving the construction of additional lanes north and south between Chaguanas and Chase Village.
The MOWI cited audit findings pointing to delays in decision-making, poor coordination, flawed project design, weak contract management, and failures to address contractors’ concerns.
According to the ministry, “when there was a contractual dispute and/or serious matters of a legal nature, it was not appropriately escalated, such as the instance of the extension of time claims from SBL (Seereeram Brothers Ltd) which is now being valued by SBL at approximately $38 million, to the Legal Department of the MOWI which could have saved the MOWI precious time and resources”.
The report also pointed out that PURE failed to notify the ministry early enough about warning signs that emerged during disagreements with contractors.
Procurement framework
The MOWI also raised concerns about the procurement framework used by PURE and the National Infrastructure Development Company Ltd (Nipdec).
According to the investigation, evaluation committees responsible for reviewing bids consisted almost exclusively of PURE and Nipdec personnel, with no representation from ministry officials, legal officers, procurement specialists or external experts.
The letter to Phillip argued that such arrangements reduced transparency and created what it described as an “insular ecosystem” vulnerable to actual or perceived bias and conflicts of interest.
Additionally, auditors questioned the absence of reports from Nipdec’s Project Definition and Advisory Committee, commonly referred to as PDAC, despite indications that the committee was responsible for reviewing procurement recommendations.
“The production of said reports was not forthcoming, which brings the entire procurement process into disrepute,” the ministry stated.

title: Kamla: UNC will deliver  on promises to union allies
summary: Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar says her Government intends to honour the commitments it made to trade unions that supported the United National Congress (UNC) in the last general election, while insisting that even unions which did not support the party have benefited under her administration.
content:
UPSET: A participant in Friday’s march on Park Street, Port of Spain, displays his creative placard. —Photo: ROBERT TAYLOR
Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar says her Government intends to honour the commitments it made to trade unions that supported the United National Congress (UNC) in the last general election, while insisting that even unions which did not support the party have benefited under her administration.
Her comments come a day after trade unions and workers took to the streets, calling on the Government to honour its promises to the labour movement and raising concerns about its handling of industrial relations.
Asked whether negotiations would continue with unions that participated in the demonstration, and whether the Government regarded some unions as allies and others as hostile stakeholders, Persad-Bissessar maintained that her administration had already delivered benefits to unions regardless of their political affiliations.
“Of course we plan to fulfil the promises we made to the unions who supported us in the general election,” she told the Sunday Express.
She pointed to the Trinidad and Tobago Unified Teachers’ Association (TTUTA) as an example of a union that had benefited despite not supporting the UNC.
“Even unions who didn’t support us such as TTUTA have already benefited. Imagine TTUTA actually got their salary increases and backpay,” she said.
However, Persad-Bissessar accused some union leaders of allowing political and racial animosity towards the governing party to influence their actions.
“That’s why I say the intentions are mired in political and racial hatred towards the UNC,” she said.
The Prime Minister urged union leaders she described as hostile to abandon what she characterised as self-promotion and instead focus on securing benefits for their members.
“Hostile union leaders should stop seeking self-promotion and work with the Government to benefit their members,” she said.
Haters and racists
Meanwhile, Persad-Bissessar has dismissed claims that a photograph she uploaded of a sparsely attended trade union protest was doctored, insisting the demonstration attracted no more than 450 people at its peak.
Responding to questions about critics who challenged the photograph’s accuracy, Persad-Bissessar launched a sharp attack on the protest’s organisers and supporters, accusing them of political and racial hostility towards the UNC.
“Move on, haters and racists, your protest bust badly, the population doesn’t want any part of your racial and political hatred,” the Prime Minister said, insisting that at its peak, “there were 400 to 450 persons and a hundred thousand ghosts”.
Persad-Bissessar also issued a pointed message to the protesters, telling them to return to work tomorrow, while making a sarcastic reference to the “ghosts” she claimed were associated with the demonstration.
Her comments follow the protest, during which trade unions and workers called on the Government to honour its commitments to the labour movement. The demonstration has since become a point of contention, with questions raised about the size of the turnout and the Government’s characterisation of the protest.
On another issue, Persad-Bissessar said she would seek further information about the water restrictions implemented by the Water and Sewerage Authority (WASA) in Tobago, which reportedly failed to prevent patrons at the Stink and Dutty event from being sprayed with water from hoses.
Asked whether she had any thoughts on the restrictions and the apparent continued use of water at the event, the Prime Minister said she was not yet certain whether WASA-supplied water or water from a river had been used.
“I have to confirm details first because I am not sure if WASA water was used or some dirty river water,” she said.
The PM also questioned the practice of allowing revellers to be sprayed with water at such events, saying, “I am always amazed that people allow themselves to be sprayed down with water in these fetes because no one really knows where that water is coming from most times.”

title: Keeping the faith
summary: Ravi B (Ravi Bissambhar) had a deeply personal reason for recording “Achutam Keshavam”.
author: Michael Mondezie
content:
BRINGING TALENTS TOGETHER: Ravi B joins Nisha B, Nishard M, Katelin Sultan, Akshay Khandoo and Peggy Supersad in the music video for “Achutam
Keshavam”, a devotional offering honouring his late father.
Ravi B (Ravi Bissambhar) had a deeply personal reason for recording “Achutam Keshavam”.
He wanted to honour his late father, Jeewanlal Bissambhar, with a devotional offering to Lord Krishna.
But what began as a personal tribute grew into a six-voice collaboration, bringing together his sister Nisha B, two-time Chutney Soca Monarch Nishard M (Nishard Mayrhoo), 2023 Chutney Soca Queen Katelin Sultan, now 12, former Children of Mastana standout Akshay Khandoo, and Bollywood singer and musician Peggy Supersad.
Ravi hoped the collaboration would accomplish something beyond the music.
“I wanted to show the world that even within the Indo-Caribbean music industry, many of us are genuinely friends and share a bond that’s more like family,” Ravi B said. “I think fans sometimes forget that because they’re so accustomed to seeing us working, competing and performing on different stages.”
An offering from the heart
Ravi B made a commitment some years ago to release a bhajan annually. Previous offerings honoured Mother Lakshmi, Lord Ganesh and Lord Hanuman.
“‘Achutam Keshavam’ has always been a bhajan close to my heart and I’ve wanted to record my own rendition for quite some time,” Ravi B revealed. “More importantly, I wanted to dedicate this offering to Lord Krishna in honour of my father as Krishna is regarded as the Lord of all souls.”
His original intention was to release the song before Pitru Paksha, a period of remembrance for ancestors. The idea grew after his manager, Vaneeta Gobin, suggested bringing different artistes together, and the recording was eventually released during Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival honouring the Divine Mother, particularly Goddess Durga.
For Ravi, the transition between devotional and popular music comes naturally. “Bhajans are actually where my musical journey began as a child,” Ravi B added. “I can celebrate my faith, embrace my culture and entertain people through different styles of music while remaining true to myself.”
Making room for others
The recording was arranged to give each artiste a verse and chorus before the six joined for the final choruses.
Ravi said he, Nisha and Nishard deliberately took guiding roles, allowing the younger Katelin, Akshay and Peggy to shine. “There was no room for egos because we all understood that this project was about something much bigger than any one of us. It was about unity, mentorship and creating something meaningful together,” Ravi B said.
Ravi recalled growing up with platforms such as Mastana Bahar and expressed concern that young artistes, particularly those under 18, have fewer opportunities today.
“I can’t consider myself a leader in this industry if I’m not doing my part to nurture the next generation and help carry our musical heritage forward,” Ravi B said.
Young Katelin has experienced that commitment firsthand.
“From the time I was just a six-year-old girl with a big dream, Uncle Ravi B took me under his wings. He believed in me and even gave me the opportunity to perform on international stages with him,” Katelin told Kitcharee. “This is my first ever group project, so it was extra special for me.”
The collaboration also stirred fond memories for Nisha B.
“Bhajans have always been a key foundation genre of music. In fact, when Karma was founded, one of the first albums we did was Karma Mangalam, a full album of devotional songs,” Nisha B said. “I actually got my break at Divali time.”
Divali also brings memories of her father and grandparents. The video shoot, meanwhile, gave her another moment to treasure. “We all came together and danced on screen,” Nisha added. “It was such a happy, pure moment of unity.”
Faith in harmony
Peggy Supersad’s connection to the bhajan stretches back to her childhood.
“I remember every Divali morning I would awaken to the sounds of classic devotional bhajans playing and the scent of sweet rice boiling on the stove while my mother began preparations for the day ahead,” Peggy recalled.
The recording itself provided another memory to cherish at Maha Productions.
“Ravi had this brilliant idea that the six of us should be behind the microphone at the same time during the recording of the chorus pieces and the outcome, I think, blew us all away,” she said. “It was practically surreal with a sense of divinity at the same time—even us artistes couldn’t believe what we were hearing was something local.”
Akshay Khandoo found particular significance in the words of his verse.
“My verse, ‘Yaad aayegi unko kabhi na kabhi, Prabhu darshan toh denge kabhi na kabhi,’ carries a beautiful message of faith and patience, trusting that the Lord will bless us with His presence in His own time,” Akshay said.
“Personally, singing a bhajan is a form of prayer, so I wanted to sing this bhajan with that love and devotion.”
Nishard M offered another perspective.

Two Days in Mayaro (Goose Lane Editions) by Pamela Mordecai assembles a suite of new short stories from the prize-winning Jamaican-Canadian author. In interlinked narratives that guide the reader through multiple perspectives, Two Days in Mayaro creates ample space to ruminate on ageing, belonging, and the indissoluble ties between Jamaica and Canada. In its titular story, an older man, now bound to a physical care facility, reflects on his life in all its myriad possibilities.
Afroalgorhythms (Columbia University Press) by Puerto Rican Yolanda Arroyo Pizarro, translated by Achy Obejas, maps and channels pathways towards an Afrofeminist future, in language that is steeped in the lyrical and the poetic. Afroalgorhythms journeys towards radical imaginings rooted in reciprocity, reparation, and the centring of Black diasporic, Caribbean and queer lives. The so-called margins of society are not only made central in this work; they are prized as originary sites of activism and resistance.
All the Hidden Places (Blackstone Publishing) by US Virgin Islander Cadwell Turnbull is the novelist’s debut short story collection. In stories that range from the postapocalyptic to the fantastical, Turnbull presents protagonists who frequently straddle the borderlines of their moral frameworks. Human complexity is critical to All the Hidden Places, with large-scale questions on ethics, survival, and the structure of civilisation rippling through these narratives. This page-turning collection is certain to inspire sustained, rich discussion.
Lahcim II: Sounds from Sorrow Hill (self-published) by Phebe Wallerson won Second Prize and Prize for the Best First Book in the 2025 Guyana Prize for Poetry. The collection, assured and measured in voice, is a study in grief and perseverance. Lahcim II: Sounds from Sorrow Hill draws deep and personal references from the community of Bartica, and the broader Guyanese landscape, to give mourning a tapestry of identity that is firmly oriented in place.
What the Forest Devours (The Borough Press/HarperVia) by Cuban Elaine Vilar Madruga, translated by Kevin Gerry Dunn delves deep—with disturbing, sinister overtones—into Caribbean Gothic horror. The women of a dense rainforest community must regularly sacrifice their children to appease a vengeful entity: the forest itself. By turns heartbreaking and ferocious, What the Forest Devours peers unblinkingly into the abyss of difficult, often traumatising decisions mothers make in the name of love.

T&T’s new Poet Laureate
Poet and visual artist Danielle Boodoo-Fortuné was named the new Poet Laureate of Trinidad and Tobago in a ceremony hosted by Circle of Poets of Trinidad and Tobago and the National Library and Information System Authority (NALIS). The Poet Laureate programme, currently under the patronage of Her Excellency Christine Kangaloo ORTT, President of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago, will run for a set term of two years.
The President’s official speech at the installation of the new Poet Laureate charged the incoming office holder to “speak in a voice unmistakably your own. Tell us what is beautiful and what is broken. Praise us when praise is due, and disturb us when conscience requires it. Help the country hear voices it might otherwise miss”.
Boodoo-Fortuné won the 2015 Hollick Arvon Caribbean Writers Prize and Wasafiri New Writing Prize, and the 2019 OCM Bocas Prize for Caribbean Literature for Poetry for her debut collection, Doe Songs (Peepal Tree Press). Her responsibilities as Poet Laureate will include public nationwide engagements, including community outreach, workshops, media appearances, and more. The programme’s previous Laureate, Paul Keens-Douglas, served from 2017 to 2026 in the role.

PreFitTT hosted the final session, a full-body workout, on October 15. More than 360 people from across Trinidad registered to participate in the sessions.
The hotel partnered with three local fitness and wellness groups to host complimentary hour-long exercise sessions.

content:
Jeremiah Reyes
LeAndra, André J Donawa and Jeremiah Reyes are the headliners of Silk, Steel & Strings on Sunday, November 8, at the Gazebo Garden at La Joya Complex, St Joseph.
The three-hour musical showcase will feature vocalist LeAndra, violinist André J Donawa and pan musician Jeremiah Forgenie Reyes, each bringing a distinctive musical style and interpretation to the stage.
André J Donawa
LeAndra
LeAndra is a Trinidadian-American soprano and graduate of the University of Trinidad and Tobago with a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Music. A three-time SanFest Best Soloist, she has performed at major jazz festivals in Trinidad and Tobago and Florida. In 2024, her sold-out LeAndra Live—Strings and Voice showcased her versatility, while her recent performance of “The Impossible Dream” at the 2026 National Awards further highlighted her vocal artistry.
André J Donawa is a versatile violinist known for blending classical technique with contemporary Caribbean sounds. Founder of Alternative Quartet, he performed for the late Queen Elizabeth II and has shared stages with international and regional artistes, including Heather Headley, Machel Montano and Len “Boogsie” Sharpe. In 2020, he became the first solo violinist featured on a soca riddim through Private Ryan’s Sweet Tooth Symphony.
Jeremiah Forgenie Reyes, 19, has been playing pan for 16 years. He began competing in Panorama at age eight with Phase II Pan Groove and continues to perform on the band’s front line. Currently pursuing a music degree at The University of the West Indies, he has also benefited from the guidance of legendary pannist Sharpe.
Unlike the conventional ensemble performance, Silk, Steel & Strings will showcase the individual artistry of each performer, highlighting the versatility of their respective instruments and musical backgrounds. A release from the organisers also teased that audiences might also be treated to a special collaboration featuring the artistes.
DJ Aagan will provide additional musical entertainment.

A performance built
for the moment
Fronted by Kees Dieffenthaller, KestheBand has built a devoted international following with anthems such as “Hello”, “Wotless” and “Savannah Grass”—fixtures of Carnival celebrations and dance floors worldwide.
“When Kes takes the stage at the Met, all of New York is going to feel it,” said Michelle Lewis, CEO of NYC Health + Hospitals/Gotham Health. “This is a night people will be talking about for years, and it is for a cause that will matter for generations. “Every child deserves the opportunity to thrive, and the support raised on November 12 will help us identify developmental needs earlier, connect families to care sooner and strengthen the services children need during the most important years of their development.”

title: The Kosher Nosh Brings Its Beloved Deli Tradition to Cresskill, Becoming a Welcome Addition to the Northern Bergen County Community
summary: The longtime Bergen County kosher delicatessen expands its tradition of authentic Jewish cuisine, family dining, and community connection at i…
content:
The longtime Bergen County kosher delicatessen expands its tradition of authentic Jewish cuisine, family dining, and community connection at its Cresskill location.
CRESSKILL, NJ - October 31, 2026 -A beloved name in Bergen County dining is bringing generations of tradition, authentic flavors, and community spirit to a new neighborhood. The Kosher Nosh, known for its classic Jewish deli cuisine and catering, is establishing a presence in Cresskill and offering northern Bergen County residents another convenient destination for kosher comfort food.

Located at172 Piermont Road in Cresskill, the restaurant serves residents of Cresskill, Tenafly, Demarest, Closter, Alpine, and surrounding communities. Its expansion is a new chapter for a local business with decades of experience serving families and helping mark important celebrations.
A New Location With a Rich History
Since 1976, The Kosher Nosh has been associated with New York-style kosher deli favorites, traditional recipes, and generous portions. Its Glen Rock location has long served customers seeking the familiar flavors of a classic Jewish delicatessen. The Cresskill location extends that tradition to a new audience, with options for dine-in, takeout, delivery, and catering.
Becoming Part of the Cresskill Community
The new location is designed to be more than a convenient place to pick up lunch. It offers a gathering place for families, friends, and neighbors to share meals rooted in Jewish-American culinary traditions. For residents across the Northern Valley, it also means easier access to traditional kosher dishes and catering for community occasions.
Local families, synagogues, schools, and organizations can turn to The Kosher Nosh for everyday meals, holiday specialties, and food for important gatherings. Its neighborhood presence adds another distinctive choice to the area’s dining landscape while carrying forward a recognizable Bergen County name.
Classic Jewish Deli Favorites
The menu celebrates familiar favorites such as pastrami and corned beef sandwiches, roast turkey, matzo ball soup, stuffed cabbage, knishes, potato pancakes, and other deli specialties. From a piled-high sandwich on rye to a comforting bowl of soup, the offerings reflect the nostalgic appeal of traditional Jewish deli cooking.
Supporting Celebrations and Community Traditions
Beyond everyday dining, The Kosher Nosh offers catering for bar and bat mitzvah celebrations, synagogue gatherings, holiday meals, shiva meals, corporate functions, and family occasions. Deli platters and traditional specialties help make it a convenient resource for hosts throughout Cresskill and neighboring towns.
A Promising Addition to Northern Bergen County
As the restaurant continues building relationships in Cresskill, its combination of recognizable dishes, local heritage, and accessible dining options gives it the potential to become a lasting neighborhood favorite. The expansion shows how an established local restaurant can grow while preserving the traditions and connections that define its identity.
The Kosher Nosh’s arrival in Cresskill is more than a business expansion: it is a continuation of a Bergen County tradition of food, hospitality, and community.

title: Notes from Afar Culture People and a Musical Language
content:
N.C., USA - October 31, 2026 -John Steffa Transforms a Lifetime of Exploration, Music, and Memories Into a Journey of Discovery inNotes from Afar
Author and composer John Steffa invites readers to experience a remarkable journey of exploration, creativity, and remembrance through his new book,Notes from Afar, a deeply personal travel journal that captures the adventures, discoveries, and artistic inspirations shared throughout his life with his wife, Nancy.
Originally documented through travel notes and reflections from their many summer journeys, Notes from Afar preserves the extraordinary experiences of two educators who sought to understand the world beyond their classroom walls. From remote landscapes to unique cultural traditions, the book reveals how each destination left a lasting impression and became a source of inspiration for Steffa’s musical compositions.
Throughout their travels, John and Nancy explored destinations around the world, including Alaska, Mongolia, Taiwan, and other remarkable locations where they encountered local traditions, instruments, and ways of life. These experiences influenced Steffa’s creative work, inspiring compositions that were later performed at renowned venues including Carnegie Hall, the Merkin Concert Hall at the Kaufman Center, and the Mansion at Strathmore in North Bethesda, Maryland.
Born and raised in Iowa, John Steffa developed a passion for music after studying at the University of Texas at Austin, where he became fascinated with electronic music and received a scholarship in music composition. After earning his doctoral degree, John and his wife eventually settled in Kentucky, where Nancy taught public school orchestras and John taught music composition. It was during this chapter of their lives that their shared passion for travel began to grow.
Each summer, the couple set out in search of new experiences, embracing opportunities to learn from different cultures and communities. Their adventures included learning about survival on an Alaskan glacier, experiencing Mongolian traditions such as throat singing, staying in a ger in Mongolia, visiting Taiwan’s mountain regions, climbing Mount Kilimanjaro, and attempting Mount Everest before health concerns required them to leave.
Following Nancy’s passing in 2022, Steffa felt compelled to preserve the story of their life together and the memories created through years of adventure and discovery. Notes from Afar serves as a tribute to a shared journey and a reminder that the places we visit and the people we meet can continue inspiring us long after those moments have passed.
“Notes from Afaris a celebration of a life shared through adventure, discovery, and creativity,” Steffa shares. “It encourages readers to cherish meaningful experiences, preserve precious memories, and recognize the lasting impact of the people and places that shape our lives.”
Through vivid reflections and a unique blend of travel and music, Notes from Afar offers readers an inspiring reminder to remain curious, embrace new experiences, and treasure the stories that define our journeys.

About the Author
John Steffa is an educator, composer, and author whose lifelong passion for music and exploration has shaped his creative work. After developing an interest in electronic music and earning advanced training in composition, Steffa spent many years teaching music composition while continuing to create and perform original works. His travels across the globe introduced him to diverse cultures, traditions, and musical influences that continue to inspire his artistry.
He is also the author of Twyla - The Early Years - 1902-1926.

title: Digicel expands device offering in push for postpaid, fibre growth
summary: Digicel Trinidad and Tobago is expanding its retail device offering through a partnership with Mobile Inn, as the telecommunications provider seeks to grow smartphone and accessory sales, postpaid subscriptions and fibre additions.
author: Vishanna Phagoo
content:
‘MAKING PURCHASING EASIER’: Head of consumer sales at Digicel T&T Ltd Romona Boisselle-Romano.
Digicel Trinidad and Tobago is expanding its retail device offering through a partnership with Mobile Inn, as the telecommunications provider seeks to grow smartphone and accessory sales, postpaid subscriptions and fibre additions.
The initiative, called Project Ascend, will see dedicated Device Zones introduced at selected Digicel Experience Stores, beginning at Excellent City Centre on November 3.
Romona Boisselle-Romano, head of consumer sales at Digicel T&T Ltd, said the initiative was intended to make purchasing devices more convenient while creating opportunities to attract customers to the company’s wider range of telecommunications services.
“One of the opportunities we identified was to make purchasing a device more convenient by bringing greater choice, expert advice and connectivity solutions together in one location. Customers shouldn’t have to visit multiple places for the device, the advice and the connectivity,” she said.
Through the partnership, Digicel plans to expand the range of smartphones, smart televisions, other smart devices and accessories available at its Experience Stores.
Boisselle-Romano said the initiative was about more than increasing the number of products on offer, as the company seeks to position its retail locations as preferred destinations for device purchases.
“Commercially, we expect to see growth in device and accessory sales, increased postpaid and fibre additions, stronger conversion from existing store traffic and greater uptake of bundled offers,” she said.
“For us, though, the real opportunity is to make every customer interaction more valuable,” Boisselle-Romano said.
Device sales experts
to be introduced
The company will also introduce dedicated device sales experts to help customers navigate device options and connectivity packages, including offers that combine smartphones with mobile and fibre services.
Boisselle-Romano said bundling was an important part of Digicel’s consumer sales strategy because it allowed the company to offer products and services that complemented each other.
“When a customer visits one of our stores to purchase a smartphone, that’s an opportunity to understand more about their connectivity needs. They may benefit from one of our postpaid plans, a prepaid offer or even fibre connectivity for their home,” she said. However, she said the approach was intended to be consultative rather than focused solely on increasing sales.
“What matters most to me is that our conversations are driven by the customer’s needs, not by simply trying to sell another product. That makes our sales process consultative, and it’s where retention follows naturally,” Boisselle-Romano said.
“When customers receive good advice, competitive value and a positive experience, we build relationships that go beyond the initial sale and turn customers into our advocates.”
She said affordability is another consideration underpinning the initiative, with the expanded device portfolio expected to cater to customers across different budgets, from those seeking entry-level smartphones to consumers looking for premium devices.
Boisselle-Romano said Digicel recognised that not every customer could afford a high-end smartphone outright and that budget constraints should not prevent people from staying connected.
“We recognise that not every customer is looking for the latest premium smartphone, and we don’t believe customers should have to compromise on staying connected because of their budget,” she said.
One option highlighted by the company is its balance parcel plan—an interest-free arrangement that allows customers to secure a phone with a 30% downpayment, spread the remaining balance over three months and collect the device once the final payment is made.
“The role of our device sales experts will be particularly important here. It’s about understanding what the customer needs, what they can comfortably afford, and helping them identify the most suitable option,” she said.
Boisselle-Romano said the expanded retail offering also supported Digicel’s broader commercial strategy, which involves aligning its retail, open-market, dealer partnership, direct sales and telesales channels around common objectives.
Although the Device Zone concept is being introduced through the retail channel, she said it could create opportunities to attract customers to the company’s other services and strengthen sales across its consumer business.
“My focus is ensuring these channels operate with common commercial objectives, consistent product knowledge, clear performance expectations and strong accountability,” she said.
Competitive telecommunications market
The telecommunications market remains competitive, with providers seeking to attract and retain customers through pricing, coverage, devices and service offerings. Boisselle-Romano said Digicel’s strategy was centred on accessibility, value and improving the customer experience.
“What sets us apart is having expert advice, device choice and connectivity together in one store. We don’t want to compete on price alone. We want customers to see the value in our network, our products, our partnerships and the service they receive,” she said.
Following the initial launch, Digicel plans to extend the Device Zone concept to its Trincity and C3 locations in San Fernando.
Boisselle-Romano said the expansion would take place in stages, with the company assessing whether each location had the appropriate device selection, trained personnel, merchandising and operational readiness.
“The goal isn’t simply to introduce Device Zones into more locations. It’s to build a retail experience that customers value and that we can deliver consistently as we expand,” she said.
Over the next 12 months, Digicel’s consumer sales priorities will include accelerating growth across its core portfolios, strengthening the performance of its sales channels and increasing customer acquisition through postpaid and fibre services.
Boisselle-Romano said the company would measure the initiative’s performance through growth in device and accessory sales, postpaid and fibre additions, store conversion and customer retention.
She added that her experience leading customer care, customer experience and commercial operations had shaped her approach to sales, particularly the importance of ensuring customers received the value promised to them.
“I’m very focused on driving growth and delivering our commercial targets, but I also believe a sale is only truly successful when the customer receives the value and experience we promised,” she said.
“For me, commercial performance and customer experience aren’t separate priorities. When we get the customer experience right and follow through every time, we’re creating the foundation for sustainable growth,” Boisselle-Romano said.

title: Cuba: the challenge of ending a dictatorship
summary: In April 1959, three months after the Cuban Revolution, a prominent Caribbean leader was asked by American reporters for his views on communism. He said, “I am not a communist (because) communism is a dictatorship and for my entire life I have been against dictatorships. Furthermore, communism means hatred and class struggle, and I am completely against such a philosophy.”
content:
In April 1959, three months after the Cuban Revolution, a prominent Caribbean leader was asked by American reporters for his views on communism. He said, “I am not a communist (because) communism is a dictatorship and for my entire life I have been against dictatorships. Furthermore, communism means hatred and class struggle, and I am completely against such a philosophy.”
That leader was Fidel Castro but, on May 1, 1961, Cuba officially became a socialist nation, having already started proving the accuracy of Castro’s description. No communist regime in history has ever delivered prosperity, peace, or freedom to its citizens, and Cuba is no exception. People might be excused for not knowing this back on January 1, 1959, when Castro and his rebels launched their coup, but every interested person should in 2026 realise that Cuba has followed the standard socialist path.
Apparently, though, this is not the case, given that anti-American ideologues still blame that country’s problems on the United States trade embargo rather than the repressive policies of the Cuban government. Yet it seems the tide is turning, albeit weakly. Last Wednesday, Trinidad and Tobago voted against a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba. According to UN News, the resolution passed by 130 votes in favour to 17 against, with 25 abstentions. This was the lowest backing for the resolution in two decades.
That shift, small as it is, was likely impelled by the more severe stance taken by the Donald Trump administration towards Cuba. The trade blockade, first imposed by President John F Kennedy in 1962, has often been more letter than law. In 1957, two years before the revolution, the US exported US$347.5 million worth of goods to Cuba; in the first part of the 21st century, that was exceeded in most years (Fontova, 2013). US ambassador Mike Waltz, says UN News, denied there was even a blockade, pointing to over US$876 million in American exports to the island in the first eight months of 2026.
This is somewhat disingenuous, however. Cuba is now suffering from an oil blockade and the threat of secondary sanctions imposed by the US as part of its larger strategy involving the capture of then-Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in January—the first domino aimed at cutting off Russia’s and China’s influence in Latin America. Cuba, because of its strategic position for launching missiles at America’s South Louisiana/Lower Mississippi River export corridor, which accounts for 25% of US water-borne exports, is a crucial part of that geopolitical calculus.
From this perspective, the authoritarian regime in Cuba therefore poses a threat to the Caribbean as a whole. Minister of Foreign and Caricom Affairs Sean Sobers, in a statement to Parliament on Friday, made a crucial distinction when he said, “True solidarity is standing with the Cuban people in their demand for political reform, democratic rights, and freedoms...not on the preservation of a dictatorship.”
How to deliver Cubans from the hands of their oppressors remains the overriding challenge.
In April 1959, three months after the Cuban Revolution, a prominent Caribbean leader was asked by American reporters for his views on communism. He said, “I am not a communist (because) communism is a dictatorship and for my entire life I have been against dictatorships. Furthermore, communism means hatred and class struggle, and I am completely against such a philosophy.”
It doesn’t take much convincing these days to realise that if ever the world was under threat from brain-eating amoebae/bacteria, just let them loose at a gathering for world leaders, and just like that the microscopic buggers would starve to death and the crisis would be averted. A few good men and women would be sacrificed for the greater evil.
Before this new week of new drama gets going let’s just take a moment to set aside our collective shame to applaud those magnificent seven Caricom countries that courageously held on to principle in standing with Cuba and its people at the United Nations last Wednesday.
On this honour roll of seven are The Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Grenada, St Kitts and Nevis, St Vincent and the Grenadines, and Suriname.
A breeze sweeps across the island, rattling shutters, scattering newspapers, and slipping through open windows. Sometimes its arrival is clear; other times, the effects are only noticed after something has shifted. Lately, it appears to have entered the same house from several different directions. The question isn’t just where it started, but why so many people sense its impact.
If I mention the name Ismael López Mastrapa, most Trinbagonians may not know who I am speaking about. But mention Keshorn Walcott, and virtually everyone will remember the young man who brought us Olympic javelin gold at the 2012 London Olympics, and continues to this day to make the country proud with his elite performances on the global stage.
Public accountability, racial equality and the equitable distribution of national resources must transcend political administrations. Professor Selwyn Cudjoe’s Sunday Express article, “Hating on black achievement” (October 25) raises important questions about all three.
Professor Cudjoe’s scholastic achievements are impressive. His Caribbean intellectual contribution deserves recognition. As a fellow Afro-Trinidadian, I take pride in his accomplishments and consider him eminently qualified to contribute to national development. But qualifications do not place anyone beyond scrutiny, where public funds and executive responsibilities are involved.

title: Heights of stupidity
summary: It doesn’t take much convincing these days to realise that if ever the world was under threat from brain-eating amoebae/bacteria, just let them loose at a gathering for world leaders, and just like that the microscopic buggers would starve to death and the crisis would be averted. A few good men and women would be sacrificed for the greater evil.
author: Raffique Shah
content:
It doesn’t take much convincing these days to realise that if ever the world was under threat from brain-eating amoebae/bacteria, just let them loose at a gathering for world leaders, and just like that the microscopic buggers would starve to death and the crisis would be averted. A few good men and women would be sacrificed for the greater evil.
Listening to the news daily, both local and foreign, no longer elicits shocked responses, gasps or any real emotions, even when it involves homicide. We have become so desensitised to the actions of our fellow men that we no longer feel involved. Gone are the days of media sensationalism, because there is no headline they can put out there anymore that will shock an already deeply disturbed nation.
I look at the leader of the so-called free world, and granted, in the past I have wondered what sort of fool would vote for a man of his standing. Now, I just accept the fact that at least half of the world’s population is “learned evil” because there is no other way to describe racists, misogynists, narcissists, sycophants, and the likes ­thereof.
Try as I might, I will never understand the origins of racism and why several centuries ago, people thought it was a good idea to enslave people of different tribes, countries, cultures, based on the colour of their skin, or economic background, or just on the way they looked or sounded. What or who gave anyone the right to enslave other human beings?
The fallout from slavery brought on many of the other ills we now face globally. Apartheid, genocide, religious wars, you name it; as a world we have seen it all and done it all. Or have we?
My only question now is: can it get any worse than what we have all seen and read about in our history books? This is what bothers me most.
We are already facing the consequences of our actions and inactions, as weather patterns change globally, something over which we do have significant control, but which will not serve the interests of the wealthy in society, nor motivate unscrupulous politicians to do something about it.
So, nothing is done. There are so many changes that can make this world a better place for future generations, but there are too many evil people out there working hard at doing the opposite.
Fidel Castro and Ernesto “Che” Guevara alongside other revolutionaries and guerrilla movements worked assiduously to oust then-president Batista from Cuba because its economy had collapsed, and its people were suffering at the hands of a right-wing dictator who they saw as showing no mercy to the Cuban people. There are some curiosities that occur when revolutionaries pursue the overthrow of incumbent rulers with the population at large remaining inured to their “rescuers”.
Since then, Cuba has come a long way making strides in agriculture and medicine, and their sugar industry today still prospers and accounts for a large part of their revenue.
While mismanagement of monies by governments will account for many a problem nations face, even we in Trinidad are accustomed to losing state funds as they pass through various ministries and politicians who seem unable to resist theft. And other than that, they are convinced that their system of governance is right; as such, their spending or looting, depending on your point of view, is justified.
It is almost a widely known fact that today’s Cuba wouldn’t be the way it is had it not been for the several restrictions on trade, etc, placed on it by then-US president John F Kennedy back in the 1960s following the Cuban Missile Crisis—a crisis that never was. But the mere boldness of Fidel to conduct talks, trade, and accept military assistance from the Soviet Union government back then is what ruffled America’s feathers.
There was no imminent threat to the stability of the region back then, just as there is no imminent threat coming from Cuba today. But the big bully in the north, the same one our leader and her Cabinet today deifies, sees it fit to keep Cuba in a state of siege, defying all international agencies’ calls for all trade embargoes to be lifted.

You are the smallest among us, yet at the United Nations you stood the tallest. As Jamaica might’ve said if its head wasn’t hanging down so low below its breath, you seven are “small but yuh ­tallawah”.
It could not have been easy and who knows what price there may yet have to be paid.
The fact that the Prime Minister of T&T stands alone in backing the continuation of the 66-year-old US embargo on Cuba should be no surprise. This Prime Minister has been nothing if not consistent in her support for US ­presidents, including on Cuba.
Even when those positions directly contradicted each other she has managed the unique feat of harmonising her position to agree with both sides.
Perhaps some of you have seen the 2014 video clip of her expressing her joy at US President Barack Obama’s decision to relax sanctions on Cuba, citing her own credentials in that regard: “For my own self, for the past four and a half years I have repeated that we should work towards getting that blockade ended. In fact just last year when I spoke at the United Nations I again called for the end of that blockade. So I feel very gratified by it because we need each other as nations...So I congratulate President Obama for doing the right thing.”
The “right thing” that President Obama, a Demo­crat, had done in 2014 and of which she approved was to decide that continuing an outdated and failed US policy did not serve the interest of either the US or Cuba, and so he switched to a policy of normalising relations.
Fast-forward 12 years to her current position which last week made T&T the first Caricom country to vote to keep Cuba under a crippling US embargo.
In trying to make sense of these two wildly contradictory positions, a reasonable person would be justified in asking “so what changed?”
Well, for one thing, the President of the US changed and he arrived singing a different tune on Cuba.
The current Trump administration abandoned its own previous policy of targeted channelling of funds to empower Cuba’s private sector in favour of a policy of “Maximum Pressure”. To a series of severe sanctions it added a fuel embargo aimed at turning desperate Cubans against their government and towards the US for quick relief.
Meanwhile, the Cuban people for whom PM Persad-Bissessar claims to be advocating against a “military dictatorship” are still waiting for the “independent” humanitarian supplies that she had promised to send them following the Caricom meeting in St Kitts and Nevis.
Other Caricom countries kept their commitments. Barbados went beyond in sending two instalments of US$500,000 to Mexico to finance a shipment of solar panels and other supplies. Other Caricom members contributed US$100,000 each.
There is no question that the Cuban people are under an authoritarian government with extreme limitations on their freedoms. However, imagine what our own position in T&T would be if we, too, were faced with an external threat backed by the military might of a superpower for 66 years. We should’ve learned that from our experience with Venezuela and didn’t, choosing instead to make history by having a red mark placed against the name of Trinidad and Tobago at the UN last week.

Any morning, one can pass the Oxford Street Clinic and witness a sight that should trouble our conscience. Senior citizens arrive in the wee hours, only to spend long periods standing in this “new level” hot sun, with empty seats outside and inside the building. This weekly spectacle has become so familiar that people can pass without a second glance. Yet behind every waiting face is a person who has worked with a public servant, raised a family and contributed to the society we now enjoy. Must these citizens endure such indignity to access healthcare? At what point did we become comfortable watching our elders standing like beggars while the very institution meant to serve them appears indifferent to their discomfort?
More troubling still is who speaks for them. Who raises their concerns in the rooms where decisions are made? Who demands an explanation for the arrangements that leave them standing in the sun? They may not organise marches, command headlines or have the strength to make their frustration heard through public demonstrations. Does that make their suffering less urgent? A society must be judged not only by how it treats those who can demand attention, but also by how it responds to those who cannot.
This is precisely why public accountability must mean more than collecting opinions. The Trinidad and Tobago Police Service has invited people to participate in a survey measuring its performance. That is a reasonable exercise. Citizens should have a voice in assessing the institutions that serve them. However, what happens after the responses are gathered? Will concerns lead to changes, measurable targets and public updates, or will they become another set of figures in a report? If the Oxford Street Clinic staff conducted a similar survey, would anyone examine why elderly patients stand beside gates that galvanise seats? Would the findings prompt a review of patient arrangements? A survey has little value if the people who speak are never shown what changed as a result.
The distinction between a well-presented institution and an effective public service is important here. On paper, an organisation can appear perfectly structured and high-performing. Reports may record targets achieved, procedures followed and programmes delivered. Yet the human experience can tell a vastly different story. A clinic can be open without providing dignified access. A public service can meet its administrative targets while the people depending on it remain dissatisfied. Institutions should ensure performance is measured by what happens to people, not merely by what appears in a report.
Likewise, workers deserve more than speeches about their contribution. The clinic issue and the labour march in Port of Spain demonstrate that wages, job security and fair treatment remain concerns. These matters belong to the same conversation about dignity, because people should not have to fight repeatedly to have their basic needs recognised.
Yet those who claim to represent the public must also examine their own responsibilities. Some executives appear more comfortable performing solidarity than doing the difficult work it demands. Public gestures and a game of dominoes may create a picture of togetherness, but they do not answer the question: solidarity with whom? Do issues disappear because a walk happened? The workers awaiting arrears? The pensioners standing in the sun? Families struggling to make ends meet? These are serious issues. They require representation, communication, and results. Without boundaries, there is no respect; without accountability, solidarity is merely a word.
Moreover, public responsibility must be reflected in public conduct. Disagreement is part of democracy, but insults and name-calling diminish the offices they come from. Children are listening, and leaders help shape what society accepts.
If the sight of elderly citizens queuing in the wee hours outside a clinic surrounded by empty seats is not a social issue worthy of our attention, then perhaps we can continue walking, talking and slandering. We can conduct surveys without acting on them, publish reports without confronting their findings, and celebrate institutional achievements while ordinary people struggle to receive basic services.
The remedies are practical. Health centres must review patient arrangements and ensure elderly citizens can access care with ­dignity. Public institutions must ­publish their findings and explain the corrective action they take. Above all, those entrusted with public responsibility must answer to the people they serve.
The breeze that opened this discussion has travelled through enough unsettled rooms. Let it change direction. Let it carry the voices of our elderly into the places where decisions are made and disturb those who mistake polished reports for effective service.
Our elders should not have to stand in the sun to remind us that they deserve respect. Workers should not have to march repeatedly to secure what is owed to them. Citizens should not complete surveys, only to wonder whether anyone has listened.
Those who hold authority today must remember that circumstances change. The elderly people standing outside the clinic were once the younger citizens upon whom this country depended. One day, those now walking past them may depend on the consideration of others. As our elders would say, “Your day soon comes.”
